claim: Six male, Long Evans rats were trained to nose poke in a central port in order to receive a food pellet from a cup below.
source: Six male, Long Evans rats were trained to nose poke in a central port in order to receive a food pellet from a cup below.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Results section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: During fear discrimination, three distinct auditory cues predicted unique foot shock probabilities: danger (p=1.00), uncertainty (p=0.375) and safety (p=0.00).
source: During fear discrimination (Figure 1A), three distinct auditory cues predicted unique foot shock probabilities: danger (p=1.00), uncertainty (p=0.375) and safety (p=0.00).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with specific probability values assigned to each cue type.

claim: Fear was measured with suppression ratio and was calculated by comparing nose poke rates during baseline and cue periods.
source: Fear was measured with suppression ratio and was calculated by comparing nose poke rates during baseline and cue periods (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodology for measuring fear output.

claim: After eight discrimination sessions, rats were implanted with 16-wire, drivable microelectrode bundles dorsal to the vlPAG.
source: After eight discrimination sessions, rats were implanted with 16-wire, drivable microelectrode bundles dorsal to the vlPAG (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure and timing in the experimental protocol.

claim: Across all 88 recording sessions, rats showed excellent discriminative fear: high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and low to safety.
source: Across all 88 recording sessions, these six rats showed excellent discriminative fear: high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and low to safety (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a summary statement of behavioral results supported by data from 88 sessions.

claim: ANOVA for suppression ratios for the total 10 s cue found a significant effect of cue (F2,174 = 592.00, p=2.32×10−78, ηp2 = 0.87, observed power (op) = 1.00).
source: ANOVA for suppression ratios for the total 10 s cue [factor: cue (danger vs. uncertainty vs. safety)] found a significant effect of cue (F2,174 = 592.00, p=2.32×10−78, ηp2 = 0.87, observed power (op) = 1.00).
evidence: This reports specific statistical test results with F-statistic, p-value, effect size, and power.

claim: Paired t-tests confirmed differing ratios for danger vs. uncertainty (t87 = 12.36, p=7.44×10−21) and uncertainty vs. safety (t87 = 20.85, p=3.50×10−35).
source: Paired t-tests confirmed differing ratios for each cue (danger vs. uncertainty, t87 = 12.36, p=7.44×10−21; uncertainty vs. safety, t87 = 20.85, p=3.50×10−35).
evidence: This reports post-hoc statistical comparisons with specific test statistics and p-values.

claim: The mean suppression ratio to uncertainty was closer to danger than to safety, despite uncertainty's shock probability being closer to safety.
source: While the foot shock probability associated with uncertainty was closer to safety: danger (p=1.00) >> uncertainty (p=0.375) > safety (p=0.00); the mean suppression ratio to uncertainty was closer to danger: danger (ratio = 0.80) > uncertainty (ratio = 0.53) >> safety (ratio = 0.03).
evidence: This describes the non-linear relationship between shock probability and behavioral output with specific values.

claim: The non-linear relationship between shock probability and behavior is critical for regression analyses that seek to determine if single-unit firing is better captured by threat probability or fear output.
source: The non-linear relationship between shock probability and behavior will be critical for regression analyses that seek to determine if single-unit firing is better captured by threat probability or fear output.
evidence: This is a statement about the analytical approach and its rationale.

claim: When the total cue period was divided into 10, 1 s intervals, discrimination was observed in each interval.
source: When the total cue period was divided into 10, 1 s intervals, discrimination was observed in each interval and its pattern showed subtle change over cue presentation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes temporal analysis of behavioral discrimination.

claim: ANOVA for suppression ratios with factors cue and interval found a significant effect of cue (F2,174 = 489.40, p=3.59×10−72, ηp2 = 0.85, op = 1.00) and a cue x interval interaction (F18,1566 = 6.21, p=5.90×10−15, ηp2 = 0.07, op = 1.00).
source: ANOVA for suppression ratios [factors: cue (danger vs. uncertainty vs. safety) and interval (1-10)] found a significant effect of cue (F2,174 = 489.40, p=3.59×10−72, ηp2 = 0.85, op = 1.00) and a cue x interval interaction (F18,1566 = 6.21, p=5.90×10−15, ηp2 = 0.07, op = 1.00).
evidence: This reports statistical results for temporal analysis of behavior.

claim: Suppression ratios are artificially high when calculated in short intervals, making for a poor measure of absolute fear.
source: Suppression ratios are artificially high when calculated in short intervals, making for a poor measure of absolute fear (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the properties of the suppression ratio measure.

claim: Artificial skewing of suppression ratios is observed equally to all cues, making suppression ratios in short intervals a valid, relative measure of fear.
source: However, this artificial skewing is observed equally to all cues, making suppression ratios in short intervals a valid, relative measure of fear.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion about the validity of the measure for relative comparisons.

claim: 245 neurons were recorded in six rats over 88 fear discrimination sessions.
source: We recorded the activity of 245 neurons in six rats over 88 fear discrimination sessions.
evidence: This reports the total sample size for neural recordings.

claim: A previous study optogenetically identified vlPAG glutamate neurons (vGluT2+) as having low baseline firing rates, compared to GABA neurons (Gad1+) that exhibited high baseline firing rates.
source: A previous study optogenetically identified vlPAG glutamate neurons (vGluT2+) as having low baseline firing rates, compared to GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) neurons (Gad1+) that exhibited high baseline firing rates (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites a previous study to provide context for the clustering approach.

claim: K-means clustering using baseline firing rate and waveform characteristics separated all neurons into one of two clusters purely on the basis of baseline firing rate.
source: We performed k-means clustering for all 245 neurons using baseline firing rate and the waveform characteristics: amplitude ratio and half the duration (Roesch et al., 2007). All neurons separated into one of two clusters purely on the basis of baseline firing rate (Figure 1E), with majority of neurons falling into the low firing rate (LFR) cluster (n = 199) and the remaining in the high firing rate (HFR) cluster (n = 46).
evidence: This describes the clustering analysis results with specific cluster sizes.

claim: Previous studies have identified a population of vlPAG neurons showing short-latency firing increases to auditory cues paired with foot shock.
source: Previous studies have identified a population of vlPAG neurons showing short-latency firing increases to auditory cues paired with foot shock (Tovote et al., 2016; Watson et al., 2016; Ozawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This cites multiple previous studies to establish context for the current findings.

claim: 29 neurons (obtained from 5/6 rats, ~12% of all neurons recorded) showed phasic increases in firing to danger, uncertainty, or safety.
source: We identified 29 neurons (obtained from 5/6 rats, ~12% of all neurons recorded) with phasic increases in firing to danger, uncertainty, or safety (t-test for firing rate, baseline [2 s prior to cue onset] vs. first 1 s cue interval, p<0.017, Bonferroni correction for three tests).
evidence: This reports the identification of a specific neural population with statistical criteria.

claim: All 29 Onset neurons belonged to the LFR cluster.
source: All 29 neurons belonged to the LFR cluster and these neurons are referred to as the Onset population (single-unit example, Figure 1F; information for each Onset neuron's waveform, firing characteristics, subject and session can be found in Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the cluster membership of the Onset population.

claim: 17 neurons increased firing to at least one cue during the last 1 s cue interval.
source: Consistent with the most recent report (Ozawa et al., 2017), 17 neurons increased firing to at least one cue during the last 1 s cue interval (interval > baseline, p<0.017).
evidence: This reports identification of neurons with late-cue responses, citing a previous study.

claim: Three neurons with late-cue responses belonged to the high firing cluster and are likely a unique class of neurons.
source: Three neurons belonged to the high firing cluster and are likely a unique class of neurons (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5 for a full analysis).
evidence: This identifies a small subset of neurons with distinct properties.

claim: 14 neurons (obtained from 4/6 rats, ~6% of all neurons recorded) with late-cue responses belonged to the LFR cluster and are referred to as the Ramping population.
source: The remaining 14 neurons (obtained from 4/6 rats, ~6% of all neurons recorded) belonged to the LFR cluster and are referred to as the Ramping population (single-unit example, Figure 1G; information for each Ramping neuron's waveform, firing characteristics, subject and session can be found in Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This defines the Ramping population with specific numbers and references to supporting figures.

claim: Differential firing was observed in Onset neurons at the single-unit and population levels.
source: Despite identifying neurons without regard for relative firing to the three cues, differential firing was observed in Onset neurons at the single-unit (Figure 1F) and population (Figure 2A) levels.
evidence: This describes a key finding about differential neural responses.

claim: Onset neurons sharply increased activity during the first 1 s cue interval, with greatest firing to danger, lesser firing to uncertainty, and least firing to safety.
source: Onset neurons (n = 29) sharply increased activity during the first 1 s cue interval, with greatest firing to danger, lesser firing to uncertainty, and least firing to safety (Figure 2B, Left).
evidence: This describes the temporal and cue-specific firing pattern of Onset neurons.

claim: The differential firing pattern of Onset neurons diminished as cue presentation proceeded and was absent by the last 1 s cue interval.
source: The differential firing pattern diminished as cue presentation proceeded and was absent by the last 1 s cue interval (Figure 2B, Right).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of Onset neuron firing.

claim: ANOVA for normalized firing rate of Onset neurons revealed main effects of cue and bin (Fs > 9, ps<0.01, ηp2 > 0.20, op > 0.95) and a cue x bin interaction (F218,6104 = 1.94, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.06, op = 1.00).
source: ANOVA for normalized firing rate (Z-score transformation) for the 29 Onset neurons [data from Figure 2A; factors: cue (danger vs. uncertainty vs. safety) and bin (100 ms: 1 s prior to cue onset through 10 s cue)] revealed main effects of cue and bin (Fs > 9, ps<0.01, ηp2 > 0.20, op > 0.95) but most critically, a cue x bin interaction (F218,6104 = 1.94, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.06, op = 1.00).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of Onset neuron firing patterns.

claim: Onset neurons showed significantly greater firing to danger compared to uncertainty in the first 1 s cue interval (t28 = 4.54, p=9.70×10−5).
source: Consistent with the ANOVA interaction, Onset neurons showed significantly greater firing to danger compared to uncertainty in the first 1 s cue interval (t28 = 4.54, p=9.70×10−5).
evidence: This reports a specific post-hoc comparison with test statistics.

claim: Numerically greater firing to uncertainty over safety in Onset neurons failed to reach significance in the first 1 s interval (t28 = 1.37, p=0.18).
source: While numerically greater firing to uncertainty over safety failed to reach significance in the first 1 s interval (t28 = 1.37, p=0.18), ANOVA restricted to uncertainty and safety (100 ms: 1 s prior to cue onset through first 5 s of the cue) revealed a significant cue x bin interaction (F59,1652 = 1.50, p=0.01, ηp2 = 0.051, op = 1.00).
evidence: This reports a non-significant comparison followed by a more detailed analysis.

claim: Differential firing was not observed in Onset neurons to danger vs. uncertainty (t28 = 1.69, p=0.10) or to uncertainty vs. safety (t28 = 0.60, p=0.55) in the last 1 s cue interval.
source: Differential firing was not observed to danger vs. uncertainty (t28 = 1.69, p=0.10) or to uncertainty vs. safety (t28 = 0.60, p=0.55) in the last 1 s cue interval.
evidence: This reports non-significant comparisons for late-cue firing.

claim: Selective firing was observed in Ramping neurons at the single-unit and population levels.
source: Selective firing was observed in Ramping neurons at the single-unit (Figure 1G) and population (Figure 2C) levels.
evidence: This describes differential firing in the Ramping population.

claim: Ramping neurons did not increase firing to any cue during the first 1 s cue interval.
source: Ramping neurons (n = 14) did not increase firing to any cue during the first 1 s cue interval (Figure 2D, Left).
evidence: This describes the early-cue firing pattern of Ramping neurons.

claim: Ramping neuron activity ramped over cue presentation with greatest firing observed during the last 1 s cue interval.
source: Instead, activity ramped over cue presentation with greatest firing observed during the last 1 s cue interval (Figure 2D, Right).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of Ramping neuron firing.

claim: Ramping activity was most apparent to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and absent to safety.
source: Ramping activity was most apparent to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and absent to safety.
evidence: This describes the cue-specific pattern of Ramping neuron firing.

claim: ANOVA for normalized firing rate of Ramping neurons revealed main effects of cue and bin (Fs >60, ps <0.01, ηp2 > 0.40, op = 1.00) and a cue x bin interaction (F218,2834 = 4.33, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.24, op = 1.00).
source: ANOVA for normalized firing rate for the 14 Ramping neurons [data from Figure 2C; factors: cue (danger vs. uncertainty vs. safety) and bin (100 ms: 1 s prior to cue onset through 10 s cue)] revealed main effects of cue and bin (Fs >60, ps <0.01, ηp2 > 0.40, op = 1.00) and a cue x bin interaction (F218,2834 = 4.33, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.24, op = 1.00).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of Ramping neuron firing patterns.

claim: Ramping neurons showed no significant differences in firing to danger vs. uncertainty (t13 = 0.62, p=0.55) or uncertainty vs. safety (t13 = 0.24, p=0.81) in the first 1 s cue interval.
source: Illustrative of the ANOVA interaction, Ramping neurons showed no significant differences in firing to danger vs. uncertainty (t13 = 0.62, p=0.55) or uncertainty vs. safety (t13 = 0.24, p=0.81) in the first 1 s cue interval.
evidence: This reports non-significant comparisons for early-cue firing in Ramping neurons.

claim: Ramping neurons showed differential firing to danger vs. uncertainty (t13 = 3.17, p=7.41×10−3) and uncertainty vs. safety (t13 = 8.26, p=2.00×10−6) in the last 1 s cue interval.
source: However, differential firing to danger vs. uncertainty (t13 = 3.17, p=7.41×10−3), and uncertainty vs. safety (t13 = 8.26, p=2.00×10−6), was observed in the last 1 s cue interval.
evidence: This reports significant comparisons for late-cue firing in Ramping neurons.

claim: Differential firing in Ramping neurons was determined by the time of departure from safety, as opposed to the rate of increase.
source: Differential firing was determined by the time of departure from safety, as opposed to the rate of increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the sliding window analysis about the mechanism of differential firing.

claim: Ramping activity to danger emerged earlier (2.8 s following cue onset for p<0.05; 5.8 s for full Bonferroni correction) than ramping activity to uncertainty (5.7 s following cue onset; 6.5 s for full Bonferroni correction).
source: Ramping activity to danger emerged earlier (Figure 2E; 2.8 s following cue onset for p<0.05; 5.8 s for full Bonferroni correction, p<0.00025 [0.05/200]) than ramping activity to uncertainty (5.7 s following cue onset; 6.5 s for full Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This reports specific timing of when differential firing emerged with statistical thresholds.

claim: Change in firing rate did not differ between danger and uncertainty in Ramping neurons.
source: Change in firing rate did not differ between danger and uncertainty (Figure 2E, Inset).
evidence: This reports a comparison of firing rate changes.

claim: Four Onset-Ramping pairs were recorded in the same session.
source: We identified four Onset-Ramping pairs recorded in the same session.
evidence: This reports the number of simultaneously recorded neuron pairs.

claim: Trial-by-trial variations in firing over each 1 s cue interval were not negatively correlated for any of the four Onset-Ramping pairs.
source: We then asked if trial-by-trial variations in firing over each 1 s cue interval were negatively correlated for any of the four pairs. We failed to uncover such a relationship (Figure 3), demonstrating that Onset and Ramping populations are distinct and independent.
evidence: This reports the results of correlation analysis between neuron pairs.

claim: Onset and Ramping populations are distinct and independent.
source: We failed to uncover such a relationship (Figure 3), demonstrating that Onset and Ramping populations are distinct and independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of negative correlation between paired neurons.

claim: Danger and uncertainty firing in Onset neurons were correlated, and single-units were biased towards greater firing to danger.
source: Danger and uncertainty firing were correlated, and single-units were biased towards greater firing to danger (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the relationship between firing to different cues at the single-unit level.

claim: Uncertainty and safety firing in Onset neurons were correlated; however, the single-unit bias towards greater firing to uncertainty was not significant.
source: Uncertainty and safety firing were also correlated; however, the single-unit bias towards greater firing to uncertainty was not significant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes another comparison of cue-specific firing at the single-unit level.

claim: Onset single-units were biased towards greater firing to danger in the first 1 s cue interval compared to the last interval, and there was no correlation between firing in the two epochs.
source: Underscoring their specificity to cue onset, single-units were biased towards greater firing to danger in the first 1 s cue interval compared to the last interval, and there was no correlation between firing in the two epochs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the temporal specificity of Onset neuron firing.

claim: The most common firing pattern for Onset neurons in the first 1 s interval was danger > uncertainty > safety (n = 14), which was the only pattern to contain more units than would be expected by chance.
source: Examining relative cue firing for each Onset neuron in the first 1 s interval revealed the most common pattern to be: danger > uncertainty > safety (n = 14). This was the only pattern to contain more units than would be expected than chance (Figure 4D).
evidence: This reports the distribution of firing patterns across the Onset population with statistical comparison to chance.

claim: Ramping neurons showed a significant correlation between firing to danger and uncertainty, along with a single-unit bias towards greater firing to danger.
source: Ramping neurons showed a selective firing pattern. A significant correlation between firing to danger and uncertainty was observed, along with a single-unit bias towards greater firing to danger (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes the relationship between danger and uncertainty firing in Ramping neurons.

claim: In Ramping neurons, there was no correlation between uncertainty and safety firing, but a consistent bias towards greater uncertainty firing.
source: Only now, there was no correlation between uncertainty and safety firing, but a consistent bias towards greater uncertainty firing (Figure 4F).
evidence: This describes the relationship between uncertainty and safety firing in Ramping neurons.

claim: Ramping single-units were biased towards danger activity in the last 1 s cue interval, and there was no correlation between firing in the first and last epochs.
source: Ramping single-units were biased towards danger activity in the last 1 s cue interval, and there was no correlation between firing in the two epochs (Figure 4G).
evidence: This describes the temporal specificity of Ramping neuron firing.

claim: The most common firing pattern for Ramping neurons in the last 1 s interval was danger > uncertainty > safety (n = 11), which was the only pattern to contain more units than expected by chance.
source: The most common firing pattern in the last 1 s interval was: danger > uncertainty > safety (n = 11). This was the only pattern to contain more units than expected by chance (Figure 4H).
evidence: This reports the distribution of firing patterns across the Ramping population with statistical comparison to chance.

claim: Onset and Ramping neurons showed no meaningful changes in activity during naturally occurring periods of nose poke cessation in inter-trial intervals.
source: To examine this possibility, we identified naturally occurring periods of nose poke cessation in inter-trial intervals, when no cues were presented. This analysis found no meaningful changes in Onset or Ramping activity during periods of nose poke cessation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), demonstrating activity patterns are specific to cue-induced suppression of nose poking.
evidence: This reports a control analysis showing that neural activity is not simply driven by nose poke cessation.

claim: Relative differences in fear do not match relative differences in firing in vlPAG neurons.
source: However, closer inspection reveals that relative differences in fear do not match relative differences in firing.
evidence: This is a key observation that motivates the regression analysis.

claim: Rats showed robust discrimination between uncertainty and safety, regardless of the temporal resolution with which fear was measured.
source: Rats showed robust discrimination between uncertainty and safety, regardless of the temporal resolution with which fear was measured (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This summarizes a key behavioral finding.

claim: Robust differential firing to uncertainty and safety was modest in the Onset population.
source: Yet, robust differential firing to uncertainty and safety was modest in the Onset population (Figure 2B, left; Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes a mismatch between behavioral and neural discrimination.

claim: The Ramping population showed stronger differential firing between uncertainty and safety, but this pattern did not emerge until the end of the cue.
source: The Ramping population showed stronger differential firing between uncertainty and safety (Figure 2D, right; Figure 4F), but this pattern did not emerge in until the end of the cue.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of differential firing in Ramping neurons.

claim: Fear discrimination was reliably detected in the first 1 s interval, indicating that Ramping neurons cannot organize fear output early in cue presentation.
source: Fear discrimination was reliably detected in the first 1 s interval (Figure 1D), indicating that Ramping neurons cannot organize fear output early in cue presentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal mismatch between behavior and Ramping neuron activity.

claim: Linear regression was used to determine the degree to which vlPAG activity is captured by fear output and threat probability.
source: To formally test the degree to which vlPAG activity is captured by fear output and threat probability, we used simultaneous linear regression for single-unit firing (Figure 5; see Materials and methods for example regression input).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used to test the main hypothesis.

claim: For each single-unit, normalized firing rate was calculated for each trial in 1 s bins over the 10 s cue.
source: For each single-unit, we calculated the normalized firing rate for each trial (32 total: six danger, six uncertainty shock, 10 uncertainty omission, and 10 safety), in 1 s bins over the 10 s cue.
evidence: This describes the data preparation for regression analysis.

claim: Total fear was calculated as the suppression ratio for the entire 10 s cue, and interval fear was calculated as the suppression ratio for the specific 1 s interval.
source: For each trial, we calculated fear on two time scales: total fear (suppression ratio for the entire 10 s cue) and interval fear (suppression ratio for the specific 1 s interval).
evidence: This describes the behavioral regressors used in the analysis.

claim: The corresponding shock probability was assigned for each trial (danger = 1.00, uncertainty = 0.375 and safety = 0.00).
source: The corresponding shock probability was assigned for each trial (danger = 1.00, uncertainty = 0.375 and safety = 0.00).
evidence: This describes the threat probability regressor used in the analysis.

claim: Linear regression unequivocally revealed that Onset single-unit activity was captured by threat probability.
source: Linear regression unequivocally revealed that Onset single-unit activity was captured by threat probability (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is the main finding from the regression analysis for Onset neurons.

claim: The beta coefficient for the probability regressor in Onset neurons was positive and significant, exceeding the beta coefficient for either measure of fear output.
source: The beta coefficient for the probability regressor was positive and significant, exceeding the beta coefficient for either measure of fear output – neither of which differed from zero.
evidence: This describes the specific regression results for Onset neurons in the first interval.

claim: Beta coefficient for probability in Onset neurons was significantly greater than total fear (t28 = 3.75, p=8.01×10−4) and interval fear (t28 = 4.57, p=8.90×10−5).
source: Beta coefficient for probability was significantly greater than either measure of fear (probability vs. total fear, t28 = 3.75, p=8.01×10−4; probability vs. interval fear, t28 = 4.57, p=8.90×10−5).
evidence: This reports specific statistical comparisons of beta coefficients.

claim: Single-unit beta coefficients in Onset neurons were positively biased for threat probability, but not for either measure of fear output.
source: The population bias was observed across Onset neurons. Single-unit beta coefficients were positively biased for threat probability, but not for either measure of fear output (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This describes the distribution of beta coefficients across individual Onset neurons.

claim: Threat probability signaling in Onset neurons was highest in the first interval, persisted several more seconds and diminished.
source: Examining the entirety of cue presentation, threat probability signaling was highest in the first interval, persisted several more seconds and diminished (Figure 5D).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of probability signaling in Onset neurons.

claim: Total fear or interval fear did not account for variance in Onset single-unit firing at any interval.
source: Total fear or interval fear did not account for variance in single-unit firing at any interval.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the lack of fear signaling in Onset neurons.

claim: ANOVA for beta coefficient in Onset neurons with factors of regressor and interval revealed a main effect of regressor (F2,56 = 7.16, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.20, op = 0.92) and a regressor x interval interaction (F18,504 = 2.38, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.08, op = 0.99).
source: Consistent with this description, ANOVA for beta coefficient with factors of regressor and interval (10 total) revealed a main effect of regressor (F2,56 = 7.16, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.20, op = 0.92) and a regressor x interval interaction (F18,504 = 2.38, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.08, op = 0.99).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of beta coefficients across intervals for Onset neurons.

claim: The beta coefficient resulting from regression using the actual shock probability (uncertainty = 0.375) was the 'peak' of the tuning curve for Onset neurons.
source: The beta coefficient resulting from regression using the actual shock probability (uncertainty = 0.375), was the 'peak' of the tuning curve.
evidence: This describes the result of the threat-tuning curve analysis for Onset neurons.

claim: The probabilities with the next highest beta coefficients for Onset neurons were those flanking 0.375.
source: The probabilities with the next highest beta coefficients were those flanking 0.375.
evidence: This describes the shape of the tuning curve around the peak.

claim: Beta coefficients for Onset neurons dropped off rapidly as the uncertainty assignment moved to the extremes.
source: Beta coefficients dropped off rapidly as the uncertainty assignment moved to the extremes.
evidence: This describes the tuning curve shape at extreme probability values.

claim: The actual uncertainty assignment (0.375) captured Onset single-unit activity better than the binary assignment (0.000) in the first 1 s interval and across the remainder of cue presentation.
source: However, the actual uncertainty assignment (0.375) captured single-unit activity better than the binary assignment (0.000) in the first 1 s interval and across the remainder of cue presentation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This reports a comparison between continuous and binary probability coding.

claim: Linear regression for the Ramping population in the last 1 s cue interval revealed that single-unit activity was captured by a mixture of threat probability and total fear output.
source: Linear regression for the Ramping population in the last 1 s cue interval revealed that single-unit activity was captured by a mixture of threat probability and total fear output (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is the main finding from the regression analysis for Ramping neurons.

claim: Ramping single-units were biased towards positive beta coefficients for probability and total fear.
source: Ramping single-units were biased towards positive beta coefficients for probability and total fear (Figure 5G), but there was no correlation between these regressors.
evidence: This describes the distribution of beta coefficients for probability and total fear in Ramping neurons.

claim: Ramping single-units were not biased towards positive beta coefficients for interval fear, but signaling of probability and interval fear were negatively correlated.
source: Ramping single-units were not biased towards positive beta coefficients for interval fear (Figure 5H), but signaling of probability and interval fear were negatively correlated.
evidence: This describes the relationship between probability and interval fear signaling in Ramping neurons.

claim: Linear regression for all ten intervals revealed that threat probability signaling was prioritized over total fear and interval fear in Ramping neurons.
source: Linear regression for all ten intervals revealed that threat probability signaling was prioritized over total fear and interval fear (Figure 5I).
evidence: This summarizes the regression results across all intervals for Ramping neurons.

claim: ANOVA for beta coefficients in Ramping neurons with factors of regressor and interval revealed a main effect of regressor (F2,26 = 8.96, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.41, op = 0.96) and regressor x interval interaction (F18,234 = 2.16, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.14, op = 0.99).
source: ANOVA for beta coefficients with factors of regressor and interval revealed a main effect of regressor (F2,26 = 8.96, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.41, op = 0.96) and regressor x interval interaction (F18,234 = 2.16, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.14, op = 0.99).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of beta coefficients across intervals for Ramping neurons.

claim: Mean beta coefficients for Ramping neurons over all 10 intervals were: threat probability: 0.58 ± 0.14, total fear: 0.12 ± 0.10 and interval fear: −0.03 ± 0.05.
source: Mean ± SEM beta coefficients for each regressor over all 10 intervals were: threat probability: 0.58 ± 0.14, total fear: 0.12 ± 0.10 and interval fear: −0.03 ± 0.05.
evidence: This reports the average beta coefficients across all intervals for each regressor.

claim: Only the beta coefficient for probability in Ramping neurons differed significantly from zero (t13 = 4.21, p=1.02×10−3) and was significantly greater than either total fear (t13 = 2.32, p=0.04) or interval fear (t13 = 4.32, p=8.28×10−4).
source: Only the beta coefficient for probability differed significantly from zero (t13 = 4.21, p=1.02×10−3) and was significantly greater than either total fear (t13 = 2.32, p=0.04) or interval fear (t13 = 4.32, p=8.28×10−4).
evidence: This reports statistical comparisons of mean beta coefficients in Ramping neurons.

claim: The threat-tuning curve for Ramping neurons was shifted right of the actual probability, with a 'peak' at 0.625.
source: Tuning was shifted right of the actual probability, with a 'peak' at 0.625.
evidence: This describes the result of the threat-tuning curve analysis for Ramping neurons.

claim: The rightward shift in the tuning curve for Ramping neurons is consistent with mixed signaling of fear output and threat probability, rather than a pure threat probability signal.
source: This is consistent with mixed signaling of fear output and threat probability by Ramping neurons, rather than a pure threat probability signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tuning curve results.

claim: Onset neurons showed negligible delay activity and little to no post-shock activity.
source: Onset neurons showed negligible delay activity and little to no post-shock activity (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the post-cue firing pattern of Onset neurons.

claim: Ramping neurons continued firing to danger and uncertainty throughout the delay period, but this firing diminished shortly after shock presentation.
source: Ramping neurons continued firing to danger and uncertainty throughout the delay period, but this firing diminished shortly after shock presentation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This describes the post-cue firing pattern of Ramping neurons.

claim: ANOVA for normalized firing rate in the post-cue period revealed no main effects or interactions for Onset neurons (Fs <2.3, ps >0.09).
source: ANOVA for normalized firing rate [factors: trial type (danger vs. uncertainty shock vs. uncertainty omission vs. safety) and bin (100 ms: 5 s post cue)] revealed no main effects or interactions for Onset neurons (Fs <2.3, ps >0.09).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of post-cue firing for Onset neurons.

claim: ANOVA for normalized firing rate in the post-cue period revealed main effects of trial and bin (Fs >3, ps <0.01), as well as a trial x bin interaction for Ramping neurons (F132,1716 = 3.14, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.19, op >0.99).
source: By contrast, identical ANOVA revealed main effects of trial and bin (Fs >3, ps <0.01), as well as a trial x bin interaction for Ramping neurons (F132,1716 = 3.14, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.19, op >0.99).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of post-cue firing for Ramping neurons.

claim: The Onset and Ramping firing patterns in the post-cue period differed from one another.
source: The Onset and Ramping firing patterns differed from one another. ANOVA with neuron type as a factor (Onset vs. Ramping) found significant interactions for trial type x neuron type, bin x neuron type, and trial type x bin x neuron type (Fs >2.50, ps <0.01, ηp2 > 0.19, op >0.94).
evidence: This reports statistical comparison of post-cue firing between Onset and Ramping populations.

claim: Onset neurons did not signal interval fear or probability at any time following cue offset.
source: Onset neurons did not signal interval fear or probability at any time following cue offset (Figure 6C).
evidence: This summarizes regression results for post-cue period in Onset neurons.

claim: ANOVA for post-cue beta coefficients in Onset neurons revealed no main effect of regressor (F1,28 = 1.02, p=0.32, ηp2 = 0.04, op = 0.16) or regressor x interval interaction (F8,224 = 0.53, p=0.83, ηp2 = 0.02, op = 0.24).
source: ANOVA revealed no main effect of regressor (F1,28 = 1.02, p=0.32, ηp2 = 0.04, op = 0.16) or regressor x interval interaction (F8,224 = 0.53, p=0.83, ηp2 = 0.02, op = 0.24).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of post-cue beta coefficients for Onset neurons.

claim: No beta coefficient for any regressor in Onset neurons differed from zero in the post-cue period.
source: Illustrative of the lack of information contained in Onset neurons, post hoc comparisons found that no beta coefficient, for any regressor differed from zero.
evidence: This reports the results of post-hoc comparisons for Onset neurons in the post-cue period.

claim: Ramping neurons signaled probability throughout the delay period, which diminished following shock delivery.
source: By contrast, Ramping neurons signaled probability throughout the delay period (Figure 6D, first four intervals), which diminished following shock delivery.
evidence: This summarizes regression results for post-cue period in Ramping neurons.

claim: ANOVA for post-cue beta coefficients in Ramping neurons revealed a significant regressor x interval interaction (F8,104 = 5.20, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.29, op = 0.99).
source: In support, ANOVA revealed a significant regressor x interval interaction (F8,104 = 5.20, p<0.01, ηp2 = 0.29, op = 0.99).
evidence: This reports statistical analysis of post-cue beta coefficients for Ramping neurons.

claim: Significant between-interval correlations for the probability beta coefficient were observed for 13/20 comparisons in Onset neurons.
source: Significant between-interval correlations for the probability beta coefficient were observed for 13/20 comparisons in Onset neurons (Figure 6E), indicating that threat probability signaled during the delay tended to persist following foot shock.
evidence: This reports the results of correlation matrix analysis for Onset neurons.

claim: Significant correlations for probability beta coefficients between delay and post-shock periods were found for only 4/20 comparisons in Ramping neurons.
source: By contrast, significant correlations were found for only 4/20 comparisons in Ramping neurons (Figure 6F); and the proportion of intervals showing a significant correlation differed for the Onset and Ramping neurons (χ2 = 8.08, p=4.5×10−3).
evidence: This reports the results of correlation matrix analysis for Ramping neurons and comparison to Onset neurons.

claim: Bonferroni correction found significant correlations for 6/20 Onset comparisons and 1/20 Ramping comparisons, and these proportions significantly differed (χ2 = 4.22, p=0.039).
source: Bonferroni correction (0.05/5 = 0.01, five tests per interval) found significant correlations for 6/20 Onset comparisons, 1/20 Ramping comparisons, and these proportions significantly differed (χ2 = 4.22, p=0.039).
evidence: This reports the results of correlation analysis with stricter statistical correction.

claim: Consistent with previous reports, a population of Onset neurons with short-latency excitation to danger was found.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Tovote et al., 2016; Watson et al., 2016; Ozawa et al., 2017), we found a population of Onset neurons with short-latency excitation to danger.
evidence: This places the current findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: Consistent with the most recent report, a Ramping population that increased activity over danger presentation was found.
source: Consistent with the most recent report (Ozawa et al., 2017), we found a Ramping population that increased activity over danger presentation.
evidence: This places the current findings in the context of recent literature.

claim: Onset activity reflected an estimate of threat probability, invariant of fear output.
source: Onset activity reflected an estimate of threat probability, invariant of fear output.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study regarding Onset neurons.

claim: Ramping activity reflected threat probability and fear output, though probability emerged earlier and was stronger overall.
source: Ramping activity reflected threat probability and fear output, though probability emerged earlier and was stronger overall.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study regarding Ramping neurons.

claim: vlPAG signals for fear output could potentially emerge at the ensemble level.
source: While vlPAG signals for fear output could potentially emerge at the ensemble level (Jones et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2018), these multi-unit codes would be composed of single-units primarily signaling threat probability.
evidence: This acknowledges a possibility while maintaining the main conclusion, citing relevant literature.

claim: Activity reflecting fear output may be found in other vlPAG populations, such as neurons showing inhibition of firing to cues, or in non-cue-responsive single-units.
source: Activity reflecting fear output may be found in other vlPAG populations, such as neurons showing inhibition of firing to cues (Tovote et al., 2015), or in non-cue-responsive single-units (Insanally et al., 2019).
evidence: This acknowledges alternative possibilities with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Signals for threat probability and fear output co-exist in the vlPAG.
source: Yet, this would still mean that signals for threat probability and fear output co-exist in the vlPAG.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the heterogeneity of vlPAG signaling.

claim: The results are correlative and Onset neuron activity may not play a causal role in fear output.
source: It is important to note that these results are correlative and that Onset neuron activity may not play a causal role in fear output.
evidence: This is an important caveat about the nature of the evidence.

claim: Previous work has found that short-latency, excitatory responses to danger are largely observed in vlPAG VGlut2+ neurons, and that excitation of this population is sufficient to produce freezing.
source: Previous work has found that short-latency, excitatory responses to danger are largely observed in vlPAG VGlut2 +neurons, and that excitation of this population is sufficient to produce freezing (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites previous causal evidence about vlPAG neuron function.

claim: All Onset neurons fell into the low firing cluster, but it cannot be concluded these were VGlut2+ neurons.
source: Though all Onset neurons fell into the low firing cluster, we cannot conclude these were VGlut2 +neurons.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in identifying neuron types.

claim: Inhibition of vlPAG GABA neurons also promotes freezing.
source: Moreover, inhibition of vlPAG GABA neurons also promotes freezing (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites previous causal evidence about another vlPAG neuron type.

claim: vlPAG GABA neurons have comparatively higher baseline firing rates and respond to danger cues through inhibition of neural activity.
source: These neurons have comparatively higher baseline firing rates and respond to danger cues through inhibition of neural activity.
evidence: This describes properties of vlPAG GABA neurons based on previous work.

claim: A causal, vlPAG signal for fear output may be observed in a GABAergic/cue-inhibited population, in concert with or independent of a glutamatergic/cue-excited population.
source: A causal, vlPAG signal for fear output may be observed in a GABAergic/cue-inhibited population, in concert with or independent of a glutamatergic/cue-excited population.
evidence: This is a speculation about where fear output signals might be found.

claim: It is clear how the observed Onset signal could play a causal role in fear output.
source: At the same time, it is clear how the observed Onset signal could play a causal role in fear output.
evidence: This introduces a mechanistic interpretation of the findings.

claim: Blocking vlPAG Onset activity to danger and uncertainty would equate neural activity to that for safety, removing the threat impetus for suppression of reward seeking, freezing and related defensive behaviors.
source: Blocking vlPAG Onset activity to danger and uncertainty would equate neural activity to that for safety, removing the threat impetus for suppression of reward seeking, freezing and related defensive behaviors.
evidence: This is a prediction about what would happen if Onset activity were causally manipulated.

claim: Recordings were intentionally made from caudal vlPAG, the subregion preferentially activated by fearful contexts in rats.
source: We intentionally recorded from caudal vlPAG, the subregion preferentially activated by fearful contexts in rats (Carrive et al., 1997).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the recording location with a citation.

claim: VlPAG manipulations that disrupt fear-related behaviors typically include the caudal region.
source: VlPAG manipulations that disrupt fear-related behaviors typically include this more caudal region (De Oca et al., 1998), and high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging reveals caudal vlPAG activation specific to aversive stimuli in humans (Satpute et al., 2013).
evidence: This provides additional justification for the recording location with citations.

claim: Threat probability signaling was observed in all recording locations (bregma −7.62 → −7.98).
source: We observed threat probability signaling in all recording locations (bregma −7.62 → −7.98).
evidence: This reports the anatomical distribution of the observed signals.

claim: The vlPAG stretches ~0.7 mm beyond the most caudal recording site.
source: The vlPAG stretches ~0.7 mm beyond our most caudal recording site.
evidence: This provides anatomical context for the recording locations.

claim: It is possible that neurons signaling fear output are restricted to the extreme caudal vlPAG.
source: It is therefore possible that neurons signaling fear output are restricted to the extreme caudal vlPAG.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and alternative explanation.

claim: Previous studies have failed to find robust relationships between vlPAG activity and cued freezing.
source: Previous studies have failed to find robust relationships between vlPAG activity and cued freezing.
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous literature.

claim: Conditioned suppression of rewarded nose poking was used to provide an objective measure of fear on two timescales and to perhaps better capture vlPAG activity.
source: Here we used conditioned suppression of rewarded nose poking to provide an objective measure of fear on two timescales and to perhaps better capture vlPAG activity.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the behavioral measure used.

claim: The measure of conditioned suppression did not capture Onset neuron firing, and only partially captured Ramping neuron firing at the end of cue presentation.
source: This measure of fear did not capture Onset neuron firing, and only partially captured Ramping neuron firing at the end of cue presentation.
evidence: This summarizes the main findings regarding the relationship between behavior and neural activity.

claim: Onset and Ramping activity were not merely driven by nose poke cessation or withdrawal from the port.
source: Further, Onset and Ramping activity were not merely driven by nose poke cessation or withdrawal from the port.
evidence: This addresses a potential alternative explanation for the neural activity.

claim: Danger cues elicit active fear responses such as escape-like behaviors like darting.
source: Danger cues elicit active fear responses: escape-like behaviors such as darting (Greiner et al., 2018; Gruene et al., 2015).
evidence: This discusses another potential fear behavior with citations.

claim: Darting is prevalent in females, but less so in males.
source: However, darting is prevalent in females, but less so in males.
evidence: This provides context about sex differences in darting behavior.

claim: The males used in this study had extensive experience with fear discrimination, and at no point was escape from the foot shock possible.
source: Further, the males used in this study had extensive experience with fear discrimination, and at no point was escape from the foot shock possible.
evidence: This explains why darting is unlikely to account for the observed neural activity.

claim: Danger cues increase arterial blood pressure and reduce heart rate, however, neither of these abilities has been linked to vlPAG function.
source: Danger cues increase arterial blood pressure and reduce heart rate, however, neither of these abilities has been linked to vlPAG function (Helmstetter and Tershner, 1994; LeDoux et al., 1988; Wilson and Kapp, 1994).
evidence: This discusses other fear-related physiological responses with citations.

claim: Danger cues enhance startle, perhaps more in line with Onset population firing.
source: Danger cues also enhance startle, perhaps more in line with Onset population firing.
evidence: This discusses another fear behavior that might relate to the findings.

claim: Dorsal, rather than ventrolateral, PAG subregions have been implicated in startle behavior.
source: Yet, dorsal, rather than ventrolateral, PAG subregions have been implicated in startle behavior (Walker et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2009).
evidence: This provides anatomical context about startle circuitry with citations.

claim: Most fear behaviors are initiated at cue onset and maintained until the aversive event occurs.
source: Problematic is that most fear behaviors are initiated at cue onset and maintained until the aversive event occurs.
evidence: This is a general statement about the temporal dynamics of fear behaviors.

claim: A substantial population of neurons with sustained firing characteristics (onset to offset) was not observed.
source: We did not observe a substantial population of neurons with these temporal firing characteristics, making the vlPAG a poor candidate for sustained fear output.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of a particular neural pattern.

claim: Any potential behavior signaled by Onset neurons must closely match shock probability, confounding this behavior signal with probability itself.
source: Above all, any potential behavior signaled by Onset neurons must closely match shock probability, confounding this behavior signal with probability itself.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the interpretation of Onset neuron activity.

claim: The predatory imminence continuum (PIC) is a highly influential theory of defensive behavior.
source: The present findings are best understood through comparison to the account of vlPAG function outlined in the predatory imminence continuum (PIC), a highly influential theory of defensive behavior (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This introduces a theoretical framework with a citation.

claim: Organizing features of the PIC are time and degree of threat.
source: Organizing features of the PIC are time and degree of threat.
evidence: This describes key features of the PIC theory.

claim: As predation becomes more imminent (pre-encounter → post-encounter → circa-strike), the form and intensity of defensive behaviors change according to PIC.
source: As predation becomes more imminent (pre-encounter → post-encounter → circa-strike), the form and intensity of defensive behaviors change.
evidence: This describes the predictions of the PIC theory.

claim: Cued fear is argued to capture post-encounter defenses: immobility elicited when predators are nearby.
source: Cued fear is argued to capture post-encounter defenses: immobility elicited when predators are nearby.
evidence: This describes how cued fear relates to the PIC framework.

claim: In the neural instantiation of PIC, the amygdala integrates information about environmental stimuli, nociceptive information and time to produce a signal for degree of threat.
source: In the neural instantiation of PIC, the amygdala integrates information about environmental stimuli (auditory cues here), nociceptive information (foot shock) and time to produce a signal for degree of threat (Fanselow and Lester, 1988).
evidence: This describes the neural implementation of PIC with a citation.

claim: According to PIC, the amygdala-derived signal is relayed to the vlPAG to organize fear output.
source: This amygdala-derived signal is relayed to the vlPAG to organize fear output (Fanselow, 1991; Fanselow, 1994).
evidence: This describes the role of vlPAG in the PIC framework with citations.

claim: Implicit in the PIC model is that the vlPAG does not contain information about degree of threat – only the resultant fear output.
source: Implicit in the PIC model, is that the vlPAG does not contain information about degree of threat – only the resultant fear output.
evidence: This identifies an implicit assumption in the PIC model.

claim: Single vlPAG neurons contain detailed information about time and degree of threat.
source: Yet, we find that single vlPAG neurons contain detailed information about time and degree of threat.
evidence: This is a main conclusion that challenges the PIC model.

claim: The results require more careful consideration of the role of the vlPAG in the fear circuit and the PIC.
source: These results require more careful consideration of the role of the vlPAG in the fear circuit and the PIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: Rather than signaling fear output, vlPAG Onset neurons signal threat probability.
source: Rather than signaling fear output, vlPAG Onset neurons signal threat probability.
evidence: This is a restatement of the main conclusion about Onset neurons.

claim: Threat probability information from Onset neurons could be used to organize a variety of fear responses, but these neurons do not intrinsically signal fear output.
source: This information could be used to organize a variety of fear responses, but these neurons do not intrinsically signal fear output.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the Onset neuron signal represents.

claim: vlPAG projections to the central amygdala (CeA) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) could inform fear output via freezing.
source: For example, vlPAG projections to the central amygdala (CeA) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) could inform fear output via freezing (Vianna et al., 2008), while projections to midline/intralaminar thalamus could rapidly relay threat probability estimates to a larger fear network (basolateral amygdala, prelimibic cortex, infralimbic cortex, insular cortex, etc.) (Vertes et al., 2015; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Buchanan and Thompson, 1994; Sengupta and McNally, 2014), promoting a variety of threat-related processes (Faull et al., 2016).
evidence: This proposes a circuit mechanism for how vlPAG signals could influence behavior, with multiple citations.

claim: Rapid threat probability estimates generated by vlPAG Onset neurons may be more akin to brainstem-derived signals for rapid detection of visual threats, which are distributed to a wider brain network.
source: In this way, rapid threat probability estimates generated by vlPAG Onset neurons may be more akin to brainstem-derived signals for rapid detection of visual threats, which are distributed to a wider brain network (Liddell et al., 2005).
evidence: This draws an analogy to another sensory system with a citation.

claim: Ramping activity could not drive fear output in full because differential fear to safety, uncertainty and danger was observed even in the first second of cue presentation, when these neurons were unresponsive.
source: However, Ramping activity could not drive fear output in full. Differential fear to safety, uncertainty and danger was observed even in the first second of cue presentation, when these neurons were unresponsive.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on the temporal mismatch between behavior and neural activity.

claim: Ramping neurons may provide a threat probability estimate that increases as threat draws nearer and peaks when threat is imminent.
source: Ramping neurons may provide a threat probability estimate that increases as threat draws nearer and peaks when threat is imminent.
evidence: This is a proposed function for Ramping neurons based on their firing pattern.

claim: Ramping neurons may help sustain threat estimates in the absence of explicit stimuli, such as in trace conditioning.
source: Ramping neurons may help sustain threat estimates in the absence of explicit stimuli, such as in trace conditioning (McEchron et al., 1998; Büchel et al., 1999), or estimate more precisely when the noxious event will occur.
evidence: This proposes another potential function for Ramping neurons with citations.

claim: Shifts toward PAG-centric activity are apparent in humans as capture becomes imminent or natural threats draw closer.
source: Shifts toward PAG-centric activity are apparent in humans, as capture becomes imminent (Mobbs et al., 2007) or natural threats draw closer Mobbs et al., 2010; with the caveat that neither of these studies could specify the PAG subregion activated.
evidence: This cites human neuroimaging studies that support the proposed function of Ramping neurons.

claim: Ramping neurons may provide two forms of feedback: the estimated probability of foot shock and a readout of fear output on that trial.
source: Ramping neurons may also provide two forms of feedback: the estimated probability of foot shock and a readout of fear output on that trial.
evidence: This proposes another potential function for Ramping neurons.

claim: Feedback from Ramping neurons could be used to adjust estimates of threat probability and fear output on future encounters with the cue.
source: Either type of information could be compared to that trial's outcome, particularly for uncertainty trials on which shock can be present or absent. This could be used to adjust estimates of threat probability and fear output on future encounters with the cue.
evidence: This proposes a learning mechanism involving Ramping neurons.

claim: The proposed feedback function of Ramping neurons is broadly consistent with a central role for the vlPAG in feedback processes.
source: This is broadly consistent with a central role for the vlPAG in feedback processes (McNally et al., 2011; Ozawa et al., 2017; Yeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This connects the proposed function to previous literature with citations.

claim: The Ramping signal could alter or reduce foot shock processing through descending control of dorsal horn nociceptive inputs via endogenous opioid circuits.
source: Even more, this Ramping signal could alter or reduce foot shock processing through descending control of dorsal horn nociceptive inputs via endogenous opioid circuits.
evidence: This proposes another potential function for Ramping neurons related to pain modulation.

claim: The proposed pain modulation function relates to the behavioral phenomenon of conditioned analgesia.
source: This behavioral phenomenon, conditioned analgesia (MacLennan et al., 1980; Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Chance et al., 1978), may be related to a more general phenomenon of placebo analgesia.
evidence: This connects the proposed function to known behavioral phenomena with citations.

claim: VlPAG activation is consistently observed in studies of placebo analgesia.
source: VlPAG activation is consistently observed in studies of placebo analgesia (Tracey, 2010; Eippert et al., 2009; Wager and Atlas, 2015; Petrovic et al., 2002) and our observation of increasing neural activity toward presentation of a noxious event may provide a suitable neural substrate for this process.
evidence: This cites human neuroimaging literature on placebo analgesia and connects it to the current findings.

claim: Between the Onset and Ramping populations, the vlPAG contains an estimate of threat probability from the time of first encounter up through the noxious event itself.
source: Perhaps most remarkable is that although independent, between the Onset and Ramping populations, the vlPAG contains an estimate of threat probability from the time of first encounter up through the noxious event itself.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings about both populations.

claim: The vlPAG may not signal fear output per se, but is rich with information that would inform a variety of fear processes and behaviors.
source: The vlPAG may not signal fear output per se, but is rich with information that would inform a variety of fear processes and behaviors.
evidence: This is a main conclusion about the functional role of the vlPAG.

claim: An ultimate explanation for non-linear fear output may be that threat systems evolved to avoid predation, not to precisely match degree of defensive behavior to threat probability.
source: An ultimate explanation for non-linear fear output may be that threat systems evolved to avoid predation, not to precisely match degree of defensive behavior to threat probability.
evidence: This proposes an evolutionary explanation for the non-linear relationship between threat and behavior.

claim: Erring on the side of greater fear to uncertain threats may promote survival.
source: Erring on the side of greater fear to uncertain threats may promote survival.
evidence: This elaborates on the evolutionary explanation.

claim: A proximate explanation for non-linear fear output may be that fear output is the summed product of multiple threat signals.
source: A proximate explanation may be that fear output is the summed product of multiple threat signals.
evidence: This proposes a mechanistic explanation for the non-linear relationship.

claim: VlPAG output to the RVM may instruct fear output to match threat probability.
source: VlPAG output to the RVM may instruct fear output to match threat probability.
evidence: This proposes a circuit mechanism involving vlPAG and RVM.

claim: Additional threat signals beyond vlPAG may govern fear output.
source: We speculate that additional threat signals govern fear output.
evidence: This proposes that other brain regions contribute to fear output.

claim: Neurons in the retrorubral field (RRF) project to the RVM, as well as the CeA.
source: For example, neurons in the retrorubral field (RRF) project to the RVM, as well as the CeA (Zahm and Trimble, 2008; Deutch et al., 1988; Von Krosigk and Smith, 1991).
evidence: This describes anatomical connectivity with citations.

claim: Preliminary data suggest that RRF neurons are primarily responsive to danger and uncertainty, but weight uncertainty similarly to danger (danger = uncertainty > safety).
source: Preliminary data from our laboratory suggest that RRF neurons are primarily responsive to danger and uncertainty, but weight uncertainty similarly to danger (danger = uncertainty > safety).
evidence: This reports unpublished preliminary findings.

claim: RRF neurons may signal threat probability plus uncertainty-induced stress, or may favor cue-shock contiguity over contingency.
source: RRF neurons may signal threat probability plus uncertainty-induced stress, or may favor cue-shock contiguity over contingency (Rescorla, 1967).
evidence: This proposes interpretations of the RRF findings with a citation.

claim: Summation of vlPAG-derived and RRF-derived threat signals by RVM neurons would produce a non-linear fear output like that observed in the discrimination procedure.
source: Summation of vlPAG-derived and RRF-derived threat signals by RVM neurons would produce a non-linear fear output like that observed in our discrimination procedure.
evidence: This proposes a circuit mechanism that could explain the behavioral findings.

claim: VlPAG threat probability signals may be trained up by the CeA, but become CeA-independent with sufficient training.
source: VlPAG threat probability signals may be trained up by the CeA, but become CeA-independent with sufficient training (Ozawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This proposes a relationship between vlPAG and CeA with a citation.

claim: The CeA is essential to the acquisition of conditioned suppression with limited training, but more extended training mitigates the effects of CeA lesions.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the CeA is essential to the acquisition of conditioned suppression with limited training, but that more extended training mitigates the effects of CeA lesions (Lee et al., 2005; McDannald, 2010).
evidence: This cites previous lesion studies that support the proposed vlPAG-CeA relationship.

claim: The CeA would not be expected to become inessential following extensive fear discrimination training.
source: This is not to say that we would expect the CeA to become inessential following extensive fear discrimination training.
evidence: This clarifies the proposed role of CeA.

claim: Updating threat probability should occur when environmental stimuli become more or less predictive of noxious events.
source: Updating threat probability should occur when environmental stimuli become more or less predictive of noxious events.
evidence: This describes when learning should occur.

claim: The CeA is anticipated to be essential to updating vlPAG threat probability signaling.
source: We anticipate the CeA is essential to updating vlPAG threat probability signaling (McNally et al., 2011; Ozawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This proposes a role for CeA in updating vlPAG signals with citations.

claim: It is near universally accepted that the amygdala is a key node of dysfunction in stress and anxiety disorders.
source: It is near universally accepted that the amygdala is a key node of dysfunction in stress (Rauch et al., 2000) and anxiety disorders (Etkin and Wager, 2007).
evidence: This describes the prevailing view in the field with citations.

claim: The focus on amygdala may be driven in part by technical considerations: whole-brain fMRI can detect amygdala BOLD signals, while detecting subregion-specific PAG BOLD signals requires a more deliberate approach.
source: This may be driven in part by technical considerations: whole-brain fMRI can detect amygdala BOLD signals (Johnstone et al., 2005), while detecting subregion-specific PAG BOLD signals requires a more deliberate approach (Satpute et al., 2013).
evidence: This proposes a methodological reason for the field's focus on amygdala with citations.

claim: The primary intellectual driver for focusing on amygdala is that it is theorized to be a privileged site of integration/learning in the fear circuit.
source: Perhaps the primary intellectual driver is that the amygdala is theorized to be a privileged cite of integration/learning in the fear circuit (Mahan and Ressler, 2012; Admon et al., 2013).
evidence: This proposes a theoretical reason for the field's focus on amygdala with citations.

claim: The present findings illustrate that the amygdala is not privileged in integration/learning, and mark the vlPAG as likely node of dysfunction in psychiatric disorders of stress and anxiety.
source: The present findings illustrate that the amygdala is not privileged in this regard, and mark the vlPAG as likely node of dysfunction in psychiatric disorders of stress and anxiety.
evidence: This is a main conclusion about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Appreciation for the vlPAG as a site of integration will hasten mapping of a more complete fear circuit.
source: Appreciation for the vlPAG as a site of integration will hasten mapping of a more complete fear circuit.
evidence: This is a prediction about the impact of the findings on future research.

claim: Deliberate study of vlPAG function and dysfunction in psychiatric disease will be essential to developing effective therapies for disorders characterized by exaggerated threat estimation and aberrant fear.
source: Deliberate study of vlPAG function (Arico et al., 2017; Assareh et al., 2017; Rozeske et al., 2018) and dysfunction in psychiatric disease (Yeh et al., 2018), will be essential to developing effective therapies for disorders characterized by exaggerated threat estimation and aberrant fear.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the clinical importance of studying vlPAG with citations.
